issues.title: SNAP: Spec needs to specify what happens when "this results in an error".
issues.author: alvestrand
issues.body:
In section 5, a number of sections have "this results in an error", but no information about what happens when an error happens.

The general principle of SDP is "if you don't understand it, ignore it" - this could, for instance, happen if a future version of this spec extended the SCTP INIT encoding so that old parsers didn't understand that it was a valid INIT chunk.

Suggestion:

Add an overall description of error handling to section 5.1:

If the result of processing an "a=sctp-init" attribute results in an error, the implementation MUST ignore the attribute, ignore any "a=sctp-init" attributes that occur later in the session, and stop generating "a=sctp-init" attributes. This ensures that incompatible implementations of this spec or any future version of it will fall back to not using a=sctp-init.

comments.author: fippo
comments.body:
Oops, missed this. In the context of WebRTC that error is "bubbled up" and leads to an error in setRemoteDescription.
This is roughly in line with the usage of "error" in https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8829.html#section-5.1.1

issues.title: DCEP acceleration
issues.author: sirzooro
issues.body: It would be nice to eliminate extra roundtrip needed to open DataChannel. Please define new optional SCTP parameter to embed DCEP DATA_CHANNEL_OPEN message in SCTP INIT, and DCEP DATA_CHANNEL_ACK in SCTP INIT_ACK. One generic parameter like DCEP_MESSAGE would be enough to handle both DCEP messages.

issues.title: Possible cleartext issue in SNAP
issues.author: steely-glint
issues.body:
If the offer side supports SNAP and the answer side doesn't, then any middle boxes get to see the clear text of the SCTP init (in the offer) _and_ the DTLS wrapped version of the same thing when it is sent over the ICE (backwards compatible) channel. This doesn't matter much in the case of star (eg SFUs) but it probably weakens the P2P+TURN use-case. 

I'm not enough of a cryptographer  to know how much difference this makes.

comments.author: fippo
comments.body: At least in the libWebRTC implementation the offerer sctp-init would not be used and different from the one signalled in the SDP. Probably worth describing that though.

issues.title: SNAP: Warning text for verification of sctp-init
issues.author: steely-glint
issues.body:
The text should make clear that the SCTP layer needs to verify that the base64 contains an Init chunk and nothing else. Specifically it should not just blindly feed the un-base64'd block into the SCTP state machine.

In the P2P use case the offer isn't seen as trusted until after the DTLS fingerprint has been verified so this chunk should not be consumed until after the certificate exchange has succeeded.

issues.title: SPED: the data rate when using PQC seems way too high, especially with multiple candidate pairs.
issues.author: juberti
issues.body:
If we're resending PQC packets across all candidate pairs every 10ms, that could be 100 * ~1KB = 800Kbps of traffic on the wire at startup, which is likely to cause problems on slow networks:

Solution ideas:
Pick "most likely to work" candidate pair (e.g., relay-relay) and send on that pair. Can this be determined reliably in all situations? Not all architectures will have "relay" candidates, and "relay" candidates typically will have the lowest PRIORITY. 
Or, simply send on the first N pairs using normal ICE prioritization, where N is capped to stay under the RFC 8445 guidance? If none of the N succeed, we can just wait until we get a successful ICE check, as in "vanilla" webrtc.
Or, perhaps a fusion of these approaches?

See https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8445#appendix-B.1 for discussion of how much bandwidth is acceptable to use (14600 unacked bytes on the wire)

comments.author: juberti
comments.body: This would be implementation guidance vs normative behavior.

issues.title: SPED: how should we do capability discovery (DATA vs ACK)?
issues.author: juberti
issues.body:
@fippo proposal:
- DATA (possibly empty) and ACK (possibly empty): SPED is active
- ACK only: we're in the closing state
- No attribs: we're done

issues.title: SPED: how should we signal termination of the mechanism?
issues.author: juberti
issues.body:
@fippo proposal:
Explicit closing handshake with no DATA attribute and just ACKs. This tells the remote side that handshake is done, regardless of DTLS version.

Closing handshake is triggered by:
DTLS 1.3 client: sent F3, got SPED ACK for F3
DTLS 1.3 server: got F3 (handshake complete on server)
DTLS 1.2 client: sent F3, got F4 (handshake complete on client)
DTLS 1.2 server: sent F4, got SPED ACK for F4

issues.author: juberti

issues.title: SPED: guidance on active vs passive setup?
issues.author: juberti
issues.body:
Generally it seems that an answer with `a=setup:passive` is better in client-server scenarios since DTLS F1 can ride with the first binding request.

Might be worth doing some tests in the simulator to verify these intuitions.

issues.title: SPED: direct send vs embedding once we have a valid pair
issues.author: juberti
issues.body:
There are some advantages to sending directly vs embedding, e.g.:
- allows larger MTUs
- allows multi-packet sends, ie PQC, even in ICE Lite
- avoids delay from ICE scheduling

If we want to retain our explicit ACK, we could combine direct sending with the SPED ACK.

This would be implementation guidance vs normative behavior.
